claim: Seven out of 8 enzymes of the heme biosynthesis pathway (ALAD, PBGD, UROS, UROD, CPOX, PPOX, and FECH) came out as positive hits in the CRISPR screen during the naïve-to-primed mESC transition.
source: Seven out of 8 enzymes of this metabolic pathway (ALAD, PBGD, UROS, UROD, CPOX, PPOX, and FECH) came out as positive hits in the CRISPR screen during the naïve-to-primed mESC transition.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results from the CRISPR-Cas9 functional screens analyzed in the study.

claim: In hESCs, only the 4 cytosolic enzymes (PBGD, UROS, UROD, and CPOX) of the heme biosynthesis pathway were highlighted in the CRISPR screen.
source: In hESCs, only the 4 cytosolic enzymes (PBGD, UROS, UROD, and CPOX) were highlighted.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results from the CRISPR-Cas9 functional screen in human ESCs.

claim: The expression of heme biosynthesis pathway genes both in vitro and in vivo is not modified during the naïve-to-primed transition.
source: In both models, the expression of these genes both in vitro and in vivo is not modified Table 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing gene expression levels.

claim: Heme biosynthesis pathway is one of the most enriched Gene Ontologies in both mouse and human CRISPR screens for naïve state exit.
source: Figure 1a displays the top Gene Ontologies (GO) for the DAVID biological processes showing 'heme biosynthetic process' as one of the most enriched in both studies (Mathieu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by DAVID functional annotation analysis of CRISPR screen data and is shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Treatment with succinylacetone (SA) during the naïve-to-primed transition significantly reduces the expression of primed gene markers Fgf5, Fgf15, Otx2, Oct6, Dnmt3a, and Zic2.
source: when mESCs are pushed for 48 hr to exit the naïve stage (EpiLC) in the presence of SA (EpiLC +SA), the expression of the primed gene markers Fgf5, Fgf15, Otx2, Oct6, Dnmt3a, and Zic2 is significantly reduced (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: SA treatment partially prevents the loss of expression for naïve markers (Esrrb, Tfcp2l1, Klf2-4, and Tbx3) during the naïve-to-primed transition.
source: In addition, the loss of expression for naïve markers (Esrrb, Tfcp2l1, Klf2-4, and Tbx3) is partially prevented in these conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Hemin supplementation restores gene expression, protein abundance, and subcellular localization of TFE3 to levels similar to those found in cells incubated without SA.
source: Hemin supplementation restores the gene expression, the protein abundance and the subcellular localization of TFE3 to levels similar to those found in cells incubated without SA (Figure 1a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR, western blot, and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1a-d.

claim: Removal of hemin during the transition in ALAD KO mESCs perturbs the exit from the naive state.
source: In accordance with the results obtained with SA, removal of hemin during the transition perturbed the exit from the naive state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: An impairment of the naïve state exit is observed in human ESCs (Elf1 cell line) when pushed to exit in TeSR for 4 days with SA treatment.
source: An impairment of the naïve state exit is also observed to some extent in human ESCs (Elf1 cell line) when pushed to exit in TeSR for 4 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: SA treatment increases EIF2α phosphorylation and reduces global protein translation, indicating activation of the integrated stress response (ISR).
source: we did observe an increase in EIF2α phosphorylation and a reduction in global protein translation, both showing activation of the ISR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b-c).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and SunSET assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: Activation of the integrated stress response with BTdCPU does not prevent the exit from the naive stage.
source: However, activation of this pathway with a chemical activator of HRI, BTdCPU (Chen et al., 2011), effectively reducing protein translation to the extent of SA, did not prevent the exit from the naive stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-e).
evidence: This claim is supported by SunSET assay and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-e.

claim: GSEA analysis shows that many crucial signaling pathways involved in development are negatively enriched in SA-treated condition.
source: many crucial signaling pathways involved in development are shown negatively enriched in SA-treated condition (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of RNAseq data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The MAPK-ERK1/2 pathway is not activated in EPI +SA cells, as shown by the absence of phosphorylation of ERK1/2.
source: On the one hand, the MAPK-ERK1/2 pathway (downstream of FGF2) was not activated in EPI +SA cells, as shown by the absence of phosphorylation of ERK1/2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g.

claim: The activin A-SMAD pathway activation is compromised in SA-treated cells as shown by the difference in nuclear localization of SMAD2/3 and SMAD3 phosphorylation.
source: On the other hand, the activin A-SMAD pathway activation was also compromised as shown by the difference in nuclear localization of SMAD2/3 when compared to the EpiLC cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1h) or SMAD3 phosphorylation (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1h and Figure 2b-c.

claim: Chemical inhibition of the SMAD pathway mimics the transition defects observed with SA.
source: chemical inhibition of those two pathways by 1 μM PD0325901 (MEKi) and 5 μM SIS3 (TGFβ-SMADi) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g-h) shows that the inhibition of the SMAD translocation mimics the transition defects observed with SA as revealed by the gene expression analysis of naive and primed markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Addition of two- or threefold increased doses of activin or FGF2 does not rescue the gene expression pattern in SA-treated cells.
source: Addition of two- or threefold increased doses of activin or FGF2 did not rescue the gene expression pattern, indicating a strong inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1j.

claim: Heme biosynthesis consumes a lot of glycine and succinyl-CoA precursors in the mitochondria, acting as a 'succinyl-CoA sink'.
source: Mechanistically, previous reports have shown that heme biosynthesis consumes a lot of the glycine and succinyl-CoA precursors in the mitochondria, acting as some sort of 'succinyl-CoA sink' (Atamna, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Heme synthesis inhibition increases the abundance of succinyl-CoA in mitochondria, which can exit the organelle as succinate and accumulate in other cell compartments.
source: We thus hypothesized that heme synthesis inhibition would increase the abundance of succinyl-CoA in mitochondria, that could then exit the organelle in the form of succinate and accumulate in other cell compartments (Atamna, 2004).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous literature and the observed effects.

claim: SA treatment decreases the abundance of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH).
source: The accumulation of succinate precursor is reinforced by the observed decreased abundance of the succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), consuming succinate in the TCA, known to be destabilized by the loss of heme (nicely reviewed in Kim et al., 2012; Figure 2e).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2e and cited literature.

claim: Butylmalonate (BM), an inhibitor of the dicarboxylate carrier, resumes the naïve-to-primed transition in SA-treated cells.
source: To test this hypothesis, we used butylmalonate (BM), an inhibitor of the dicarboxylate carrier (DIC; SLC25A10), to prevent leakage of succinate from the mitochondrial matrix to the cytosol (Mills et al., 2018), and this nicely resumed the transition as shown by the gene expression profile of mESCs in the EpiLC + SA + BM condition (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2f and cited literature.

claim: Succinate accumulation increases protein lysine succinylation.
source: Succinate accumulation and/or SDH ablation is known to increase protein lysine succinylation (Smestad et al., 2018), an effect that is observed upon SA treatment and that we mimicked by inhibiting Sirt7, a cytosolic and nuclear desuccinylase (Figure 2g).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2g and cited literature.

claim: Inhibition of Sirt7 mimics SA in preventing the exit of the naive state.
source: The ability of this molecule to mimic SA in the pathway's inhibition (Figure 2h–i) and to prevent the exit of the naive state (Figure 2f) points at succinylation events as the cause of the transition defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2f, h-i.

claim: Treatment of naïve 2iL cells with SA modifies the global gene expression as shown by PCA analysis.
source: In addition to this defect in the exit from the naive state, we found that treatment of naïve 2iL cells with SA also modifies the global gene expression as 2iL + SA samples cluster away from 2iL control cells when analyzed by PCA performed on RNAseq data (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis of RNAseq data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The expression of 142 genes previously identified as upregulated in the 2C-like population is statistically upregulated in 2iL versus 2iL + SA.
source: Indeed, the expression of the 142 genes previously identified as upregulated in this 2C-like population (Macfarlan et al., 2012) was statistically upregulated in 2iL versus 2iL + SA (Figure 3b)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 3b and cited literature.

claim: Treatment with SA increases the fraction of ZSCAN4+ and MUERVL-GAG+ cell populations by two to three folds.
source: As shown in Figure 3e and f, treatment with SA increases the fraction of 2C-like cells by two to three folds.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3e and f.

claim: SA treatment upregulates 2CLC markers in ALAD KO mESCs.
source: this was further confirmed by RT-qPCR for a selection of the most common markers (Figure 3c) and further supported by the upregulation of the 2CLC markers in ALAD KO mESCs (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3c and 3d.

claim: A similar trend of increased ZGA-related gene expression is observed in hESCs treated with SA.
source: A similar trend is observed for genes involved in the ZGA for hESCs (Taubenschmid-Stowers et al., 2022; Figure 3g).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3g and cited literature.

claim: The 2C-like phenotype induced by SA is independent of heme as it is not rescued by hemin supplementation.
source: Interestingly, and as opposed to the naive-to-primed setup, the observed phenotype seems independent of heme as it is not rescued by hemin supplementation (Figure 4a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR and RNAseq data shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: SA treatment causes a dramatic increase in succinylated proteins in all subcellular compartments.
source: However, a dramatic increase in the signal associated with succinylated proteins is observed in all subcellular compartments when heme synthesis is inhibited, an effect that is not (or very partially) rescued upon hemin supplementation (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Addition of butylmalonate (BM) combined with SA rescues both the increase in 2C markers and the proportion of ZSCAN4 or MUERVL-positive cells.
source: As hypothesized, addition of BM combined to SA is correlated to a rescue of both the increase in 2 C markers and the proportion of ZSCAN4 or MUERVL-positive cells in the population (Figure 4a and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4a and d.

claim: Glycine supplementation does not induce the 2C-like phenotype.
source: Altogether, this shows that an accumulation of extra-mitochondrial succinate upstream of heme synthesis in naive mESCs induces a 2C-like phenotype, reinforced by the inability of glycine to induce same effect (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Endogenous 2CLCs (GFP+; OCT4-) show an increase in protein succinylation compared to non-2CLCs.
source: The simultaneous observation of the endogenous GFP fluorescence, the absence of OCT4 (Macfarlan et al., 2012) and the immunostaining of the succinyl-lysine residues showed an increase in protein succinylation specifically in the 2C-like cells (GFP+; OCT4-) sub-population, as quantified by flow cytometry (Figure 4e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4e-f and cited literature.

claim: Atpenin A5 (AA5), an SDH inhibitor, induces protein lysine succinylation.
source: AA5 induces the protein lysine succinylation (Figure 5a)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: AA5 treatment increases the number of ZSCAN4-positive cells.
source: AA5 induces the protein lysine succinylation (Figure 5a), an increase in the number of ZSCAN4-positive cells (Figure 5b)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: AA5 treatment increases the expression of 2C markers.
source: AA5 induces the protein lysine succinylation (Figure 5a), an increase in the number of ZSCAN4-positive cells (Figure 5b) and the expression of 2 C markers (Figure 5c and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5c and e.

claim: Addition of BM counteracts the effects of AA5 on 2CLC markers.
source: These effects were counteracted by the addition of BM to prevent the succinate exit from the mitochondria (Figure 5b), confirming the involvement of succinate in the process.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Exogenous supplementation with sodium succinate or dimethylsuccinate increases 2CLC marker expression.
source: Indeed, exogenous supplementation with a membrane impermeable (sodium succinate) or permeable (dimethylsuccinate) form of succinate were able to increase the 2CLC marker expression (Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Inhibition of succinate exit through MCT1/4 and SUCNR1 receptor reduces the rise in 2CLC marker expression triggered by AA5.
source: We further found that inhibition of the succinate exit through the plasma membrane, by targeting MCT1 and 4 with the AZD3965 inhibitor (Beloueche-Babari et al., 2017; Reddy et al., 2020) combined to inhibition of the succinate receptor SUCNR1 by NF-56-EJ40 (Haffke et al., 2019) is able to bring down the rise in 2CLC marker expression triggered by AA5 (Figure 5e).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5e and cited literature.

claim: Retinoic acid (RA) increases the 2CLC population through a mechanism mediated by both RAR and RXR.
source: Recent reports have shown that retinoic acid (RA) also increases the 2CLC population, an effect mediated by the retinoic acid receptor RAR but not the RXRs (Iturbide et al., 2021). While the induction of the 2CLC gene signature in response to AA5 is similar to RA, the mode of action seems to involve both RAR and RXR since the effect is rescued by addition of both inhibitors, AGN193109 and HX531, respectively (Figure 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5c and cited literature.

claim: Succinate acts as a paracrine/autocrine signal upstream of RAR/RXR transcriptional activity.
source: These findings strongly support succinate acting as a paracrine/autocrine signal upstream of RAR/RXR transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing succinate effects and RAR/RXR involvement.

claim: Embryonic lethality at the implantation stage occurs in mouse embryos knockout for heme synthesis pathway enzymes HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX, and FECH.
source: This is in accordance with the embryonic lethality at the implantation stage of mouse embryos knockout for the heme synthesis pathway enzymes since the naive-to-primed transition recapitulates, in vitro, this critical step (shown for HMBS Lindberg et al., 1996, UROS Bensidhoum, 1998, UROD Phillips et al., 2001, CPOX Conway et al., 2017 and FECH Magness et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The proper activation of MAPK and TGFβ-SMAD pathways is required to proceed with the naïve-to-primed transition.
source: It has been previously demonstrated that the proper activation of these two pathways is required to proceed with the transition to the primed stage (Tsanov et al., 2017; Jiapaer et al., 2018; Senft et al., 2018; Arman et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A connection between heme synthesis inhibition and MAPK signaling blockade has been reported in PC12 neuronal cells.
source: Such a connection between heme synthesis inhibition and signaling pathways has only been reported once in PC12 neuronal cells, with SA blocking the activation of the MAPK despite the presence of nerve growth factor (NGF) (Zhu et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A small population (about 1%) of mouse ESCs grown in naïve conditions displays features of the two-cell stage embryo (2C-like population or 2CLCs).
source: Interestingly, a small population (representing about 1 %) of mouse ESCs grown in naïve conditions displays features of the two-cell stage embryo (2C-like population or 2CLCs) exhibiting extended potential (Macfarlan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The 2CLC subset displays the expression of 2C-specific genes such as the Zscan4 cluster, MuERVL, and DUX.
source: This subset also displays the expression of 2C-specific genes such as the Zscan4 cluster, the retro-transposable element MuERVL or the master regulator DUX (Macfarlan et al., 2012; Percharde et al., 2018; Ishiuchi et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 2CLCs exhibit a disappearance of chromocenters and loss of the core pluripotency protein OCT4.
source: a disappearance of chromocenters and loss of the core pluripotency protein OCT4 (Macfarlan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: mTORC1/2 is a critical component for the naïve-to-primed transition.
source: Notably, a few studies have revealed mTORC1/2 as a critical component for the naïve-to-primed transition (Mathieu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018; Duggal et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: mTORC1/2 regulates key developmental pathways such as Wnt signaling.
source: that regulates key developmental pathways such as Wnt signaling (Sperber et al., 2015; Mathieu et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2016; Taelman et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SA treatment does not increase the abundance of HIF1α, demonstrating a lack of PHD inhibition.
source: Of these three classes, we ruled out a role for PHDs, responsible for HIF1α degradation, as the abundance of this transcription factor was not increased by SA nor by AA5 treatment, demonstrating a lack of stabilization following a putative PHD inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SA or AA5 treatment increases the amount of trimethylation of lysines 4, 9, and 27 of H3 (H3K4,-K9, -K27).
source: we then focused our attention on the histone 3 (H3) and DNA methylation landscapes and observed a robust increase in the amount of trimethylation of lysines 4, 9, and 27 of H3 (H3K4,-K9, -K27) along with an increase in the global abundance of 5mC when mESCs were treated with either SA or AA5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a-d).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a-d.

claim: SA or AA5 treatment increases the global abundance of 5mC.
source: we then focused our attention on the histone 3 (H3) and DNA methylation landscapes and observed a robust increase in the amount of trimethylation of lysines 4, 9, and 27 of H3 (H3K4,-K9, -K27) along with an increase in the global abundance of 5mC when mESCs were treated with either SA or AA5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a-d).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a-d.

claim: Chemical inhibition of HDMs by JIB04 and/or TET by TETin-C35 does not trigger a rise in the proportion of 2CLCs or in 2C marker expression.
source: However, chemical inhibition of HDMs by JIB04 (Wang et al., 2013) and/or TET by TETin-C35 (Singh et al., 2020) does not trigger a rise in the proportion of 2CLCs or in 2 C marker expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2e-f).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2e-f and cited literature.

claim: Embryonic lethality of SDH subunits in mice demonstrates the importance of succinate in early development.
source: Further emphasis on the importance of succinate in early development is also demonstrated by the embryonic lethality of the SDH subunits in mice (Piruat et al., 2004; Siebers et al., 2018; Lepoutre-Lussey et al., 2016; Takács-Vellai et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Naïve ESCs resemble the inner cell mass (ICM) of the pre-implantation embryo epiblast.
source: the naïve ESCs, resembling the inner cell mass (ICM) of the pre-implantation embryo epiblast
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of stem cell biology.

claim: Primed ESCs mirror the epiblast of the post-implantation stage.
source: and the primed ESCs, mirroring the epiblast of the post-implantation stage.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of stem cell biology.

claim: Naïve and primed ESCs display dramatic differences in developmental potential, epigenetic landscape, X-chromosome inactivation pattern, and metabolic activity.
source: While these cells represent timely close stages in embryo development, they display dramatic differences, such as developmental potential (Gafni et al., 2013; Ware et al., 2014), epigenetic landscape, X-chromosome inactivation pattern and metabolic activity (Sperber et al., 2015; Theunissen et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2012; Sahakyan et al., 2017; Grow et al., 2015; Takashima et al., 2014; Nichols and Smith, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ESC culture is heterogenous in terms of pluripotent or epigenetic marker expression.
source: Aside from these two pluripotent stages, ESC culture is known to be very heterogenous in terms of pluripotent or epigenetic marker expression (Sustáčková et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The 2CLC population is transient and cycles back and forth to a naive pluripotency state.
source: Interestingly, this 2CLC population is transient and cycles back and forth to a naive pluripotency state (Macfarlan et al., 2012; Fu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Metabolites such as acetate, lactate, and D-ribose play a role in the gain of 2CLC features.
source: The role of several metabolites in the gain of 2CLC features has already been recently unveiled, highlighting a role for acetate, lactate, and D-ribose (Rodriguez-Terrones et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A previous metabolite screening showed a positive effect of succinate on the 2C-like features acquisition.
source: This metabolite screening also showed a positive effect of succinate on the 2C-like features acquisition.
evidence: This claim refers to previous screening data mentioned in the context.

claim: Succinate accumulation leads to a global reduction in cytosine demethylation activity of TETs and histone demethylation, as observed in cancers after succinate accumulation or SDH mutations.
source: Beyond its role in the cellular metabolism, we show here that the succinate accumulation outside mitochondria leads to a global reduction in cytosine demethylation activity of the TETs and histone demethylation as previously observed in cancers after accumulation of succinate or SDH mutations (Letouzé et al., 2013; Xiao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in the study and citations to previous literature.

claim: TET2 can cooperate with PSPC1 to reduce the expression of the retrotransposon MuERVL.
source: For example, while TET2 could cooperate with PSPC1 (Paraspeckle Component 1) to reduce the expression of the retrotransposon MuERVL (Guallar et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Binding of TET proteins with SMCHD1 prevents the demethylation of the Dux gene locus and thus prevents its expression.
source: binding of the TET proteins with SMCHD1 (structural maintenance of chromosomes flexible hinge domain containing 1) prevents the demethylation of the Dux gene locus and thus prevents its expression (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TET triple KO induces the 2C phenotype.
source: Succinate accumulation would result in a global decrease in the activity of all 3 TET isoforms, resembling those of a TET triple KO, already shown to induce the 2 C phenotype (Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The methylation landscape of histones, especially H3, is highly dynamic both in vivo at the time of ZGA and in the 2CLC conversion.
source: The methylation landscape of histones, especially H3, is also highly dynamic both in vivo, at the time of the zygote genome activation (ZGA) that takes place at the 2C-stage, and in the 2CLC conversion with remodeling of H3K4me3, H3K9me3, and H3K27me3 (Zhang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2022) (extensively reviewed in Xia and Xie, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of KDM1a promotes the expression of Zscan4 and MuERVL.
source: as loss of KDM1a (lysine demethylase 1 a) is shown to promote the expression of Zscan4 and MuERVL (Macfarlan et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Loss of KDM5a and b decreases the expression of 2CLC markers and blocks the ZGA in vivo.
source: whereas loss of KDM5a and b decreases the expression of the markers and blocks the ZGA in vivo (Dahl et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The discrepancy in the role of epigenetic modifications in 2CLC emergence could be due to differences in culture conditions between serum+LIF and ground naïve (2iL) mESCs.
source: This discrepancy could be due to differences in the culture conditions, as these previous studies use mESC grown in serum +LIF conditions, while we use ground naïve mESCs (in 2iL and serum-free culture). Such difference has been previously described in the establishment of another pluripotent state of ESCs, the paused state (Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on observed differences and cited literature.

claim: Metabolites such as S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), alpha-ketoglutarate (αKG), glutamine, acetyl-CoA, lactate, and D-ribose regulate pluripotent states mostly through their contribution to modifications of the epigenetic landscape.
source: Our study thus brings an additional and different example of metabolic control of pluripotency, and adds succinate to previously reported metabolites such as S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) (Sperber et al., 2015), alpha-ketoglutarate (αKG) (Carey et al., 2015; Tischler et al., 2019), glutamine (Tohyama et al., 2016), acetyl-CoA (Moussaieff et al., 2015), lactate or D-ribose (Rodriguez-Terrones et al., 2020) that are known to regulate the pluripotent states mostly through their contribution to modifications of the epigenetic landscape (reviewed in Tsogtbaatar et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Succinate influences pluripotency regulation through protein succinylation and a paracrine effect.
source: In addition to these previous studies, we highlight a role of succinate that goes beyond epigenetic landscape regulation but instead influences pluripotency regulation through protein succinylation and a paracrine effect.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Both heme and succinate play a critical role in the progression of the pluripotency continuum, ranging from 2CLCs to the acquisition of primed pluripotency.
source: Altogether, these results indicate a critical role of both heme and succinate in the progression of the pluripotency continuum, ranging from the 2CLCs on one hand and to the acquisition of primed pluripotency on the other.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: The link between heme and MAPK/TGFβ-SMAD signaling pathways remains unknown.
source: While the link between heme and these crucial signaling pathways remains unknown, it brings to light a crucial importance of this metabolite and its synthesis pathway, so far poorly understood, in the context of pluripotency.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current understanding.

claim: Succinylation events are the cause of the naïve-to-primed transition defects upon heme synthesis inhibition.
source: The ability of this molecule to mimic SA in the pathway's inhibition (Figure 2h–i) and to prevent the exit of the naive state (Figure 2f) points at succinylation events as the cause of the transition defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing Sirt7 inhibition effects.

claim: Extracellular succinate acts as a paracrine/autocrine signal able to trigger 2C-like reprogramming through the activation of SUCNR1.
source: We further demonstrate that extracellular succinate acts as a paracrine/autocrine signal, able to trigger the 2C-like reprogramming through the activation of its plasma membrane receptor, SUCNR1.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings with MCT and SUCNR1 inhibitors.

claim: The exit of the naïve state is impaired upon heme biosynthesis pathway blockade in mESCs.
source: we show here that the exit of the naïve state is impaired upon heme biosynthesis pathway blockade, linked in mESCs to the incapacity to activate MAPK- and TGFβ-dependent signaling pathways after succinate accumulation.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Heme synthesis inhibition promotes the acquisition of 2 cell-like cells in a heme-independent manner caused by mitochondrial succinate accumulation and leakage.
source: In addition, heme synthesis inhibition promotes the acquisition of 2 cell-like cells in a heme-independent manner caused by a mitochondrial succinate accumulation and leakage out of the cell.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: This study unveils a new mechanism underlying the maintenance of pluripotency under the control of heme synthesis.
source: Overall, this study unveils a new mechanism underlying the maintenance of pluripotency under the control of heme synthesis.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the study's contribution.

claim: BACH1 does not accumulate in the nucleus following SA treatment.
source: While we did not observe an accumulation of BACH1 in the nucleus following SA treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The pathway inhibition by SA was especially observed after 24 h of treatment, concomitant with the defect in gene expression.
source: This pathway inhibition was especially observed after 24 h of treatment, and concomitant with the defect in gene expression (Figure 2b–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and RT-qPCR time course data shown in Figure 2b-d.

claim: In basal conditions, the bulk of succinyllysine modifications are located in the mitochondria.
